rationale: The unsigned |ΔWC/at| conditioner is a genuinely new and diagnostically useful test of whether the archive's working-capital results reflect constraint intensity rather than direction, and the expression matches the hypothesis, though it should be interpreted cautiously since |Δ| loads heavily on small, volatile firms where gross profitability is already known to work best.

Economically coherent and the two conditioners are genuinely distinct (internal-capital stock vs. liquidity flow), but multiplying two already-tested winning conditioners is close to stacking prior results, and the product of two [0,1] ranks compresses most mass toward zero so the effective spread will come from a narrow tail whose stability must be checked.

This is a cosmetic smoothing variant of the archived GrossProfitAtOwnLiquidityTrough (identical conditioner, three-year average of the same numerator), which the objective explicitly discourages, and gross-profitability levels are already known to be highly persistent so a 3-year MA will be ~0.95 correlated with the one-year print.

The conditioner is internally inconsistent with its stated distance-to-default story: because (dltt+dlc) can be near zero, small-loss firms with almost no debt receive the most extreme NEG(pi/debt) values and are ranked as the *most* default-proximate, so the sort will be driven by low-leverage micro-caps rather than by firms with creditors to fail.

The depreciation-attribution question is legitimate and the expression matches the hypothesis, but the construct is close to a linear blend of two already-archived trough signals (gross profit at trough and depreciation intensity at trough), so its value is diagnostic rather than as a candidate final signal.

A persistent-instability conditioner is a reasonable complement to Signal 1 and is not a rediscovery of anything in the archive, but WC/at volatility is a strong proxy for size and idiosyncratic risk, so a positive result will need to be shown to be more than the well-known concentration of the profitability premium in small, volatile stocks.
